name: SesameRx
one_liner: SesameRx was Sesame's cash-pay prescription program; Sesame now offers Everyday Rx ($1 generics with a membership) and Mental Health Rx.
best_for: People without insurance who take common generic medications
People who need ongoing non-controlled psychiatric medication refills at a fixed monthly price
not_for: Anyone in crisis: call or text 988
People who need stimulants, benzodiazepines or other controlled medications
People who want prescriptions billed to insurance
short_description: Sesame's cash-pay medication programs: Everyday Rx ($29–$59/month, then $1 generics) and Mental Health Rx ($79/month). Same company as Sesame.
long_description: SesameRx launched in 2021 as the cash-pay prescription arm of Sesame, the telehealth marketplace, offering low-cost generic medications filled by partner pharmacy Truepill with no insurance needed. It is part of the same company and website as Sesame, not a separate service. Sesame's current medication offers are Everyday Rx, a membership ($29/month on an annual plan or $59/month month-to-month) that gives access to over 350 common medications for $1 each with a dedicated clinician, and Mental Health Rx, a $79/month subscription for ongoing psychiatric medication management. Medication can be delivered or, for some, picked up the same day at a local pharmacy. Sesame does not bill insurance, and its providers do not prescribe controlled substances such as stimulants or benzodiazepines.

pricing.starting_price: $29/month (Everyday Rx annual plan) or $59/month; Mental Health Rx $79/month
pricing.notes: Everyday Rx: $29/month on an annual plan or $59/month month-to-month, then $1 per prescription for 350+ common medications; past months are not refunded. Mental Health Rx: $79/month for psychiatric medication management. Cash-pay only. The original 2021 SesameRx program advertised $5 generics with free shipping.

privacy.notes: Policy says Sesame may share personal information with third parties for their direct marketing (California residents can opt out) and share de-identified data with advertisers. Provider terms require health data to be kept under HIPAA. Deletion rights for all users not confirmed. No regulatory action found.
